title: A 'Good Ear' Makes Language Learning Easier — Study
paragraphs: Why do some people find it easier to learn the sounds of a foreign language than others? According to a new study, part of the answer may lie in how precisely they can hear small differences in sounds.

The study was carried out by researchers from University College London (UCL) in the UK and Tohoku University in Japan, and published in 2026 in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: General. It was led by Dr. Kazuya Saito-van Poeteren of the UCL Institute of Education.

The researchers studied 67 Japanese people who were learning English. First, they tested how well the participants could detect small differences in sounds that were not speech, such as changes in pitch, length and tone. The researchers called this ability "auditory precision."

Next, the researchers used brain scans to record the participants' brain activity while they tried to tell the difference between two English vowel sounds. These were the vowels in words like "cat" and "cut," which have no direct equivalent in Japanese.

The results showed clear differences between the learners. Those with higher auditory precision relied less on a part of the brain involved in language processing when they heard the foreign sounds. Instead, their brains processed the sounds in a way similar to how they process non-speech sounds. According to the researchers, this may have made it easier for them to hear the foreign sounds accurately, because their native language patterns did not get in the way as much.
On the other hand, learners with lower auditory precision relied more on this language area and tended to apply Japanese pronunciation patterns to the new English sounds.

Saito-van Poeteren explained that learners with a "good ear" can process new foreign-language sounds objectively, without immediately treating them as language. The researchers believe that foreign language education should not simply focus on more practice. Instead, it should also help develop learners' listening abilities. The team now plans to create a new kind of training that combines language learning with auditory training.
